clue.text: That is to be presented by belted earl and duke in Edinburgh

indicators.note: something belted has been thrashed about, so the letters of the nobles are knocked into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
i.e., the abbreviation of id est, 'that is'

explanation.surface: A belted earl and a duke are to be formally presented at some ceremony in Scotland's capital.
explanation.walkthrough: A belted earl is a genuine heraldic phrase for a peer invested with the sword-belt, which hides the anagram signal; the IE is placed after the shuffled nobles.
explanation.definitionFit: Auld Reekie, Scots for 'Old Smoky', is the traditional nickname for Edinburgh from its smoke-filled chimneys.

clue.text: Say yes to trust and agree to buy

blocks.note: first meaning: consent to an offer or proposal
second meaning: take goods or a bid on the agreed terms

explanation.surface: Someone is told to agree to trust a seller and commit to a purchase.
explanation.walkthrough: The middle word 'trust' is a third sense of the same verb, believing something as true, so the clue is really a triple definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb covers consenting to an invitation and taking up an offer of sale, as when a dealer accepts a bid.

clue.text: See lieutenant rounding English height in the distance

indicators.note: to round something is to go all the way about it, so the officer's letters wrap around the next piece

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for the military rank
standard abbreviation for English
H is the usual abbreviation for height

explanation.surface: An officer is spotted far off, rounding an English hill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' simply invites the reader to look and plays no part in the wordplay; the officer abbreviation wraps only the English, and height follows outside.
explanation.definitionFit: Length is the measurement of how far something extends from end to end, its distance.

clue.text: Get in touch about a church

blocks.note: re means concerning, as in a memo
taken as written
standard abbreviation for church

explanation.surface: Someone contacts a parish about church business.
explanation.definitionFit: To reach a person is to contact them, as in phoning or writing to someone successfully.

clue.text: Writer in West Germany - he collapsed

indicators.note: something that has collapsed has fallen apart, so the preceding words tumble into a new order

blocks.note: every letter of these words is used

explanation.surface: An author suffers a collapse while in West Germany.
explanation.definitionFit: Ernest Hemingway was the American novelist who wrote The Old Man and the Sea, so he is a writer.

clue.text: Lush, not dried out, and drinking up as we speak, it wouldn't surprise me

indicators.note: out suggests being put out of order, so the first three words are reshuffled
in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top, back to front
drinking means taking something inside, so the shuffled letters hold the other piece

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
at this very moment

explanation.surface: A drunk who hasn't dried out and is drinking right now: no surprise there.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lush' (a drunk) and 'drinking' make a consistent boozy picture, but the drunk is only fodder; the shuffled letters hold the turned-round NOW.
explanation.definitionFit: The colloquial phrase expresses that something seems likely, exactly the sense of saying it would not surprise me.

clue.text: Shot in chest, a bombardier

indicators.note: in tells the solver the letters lie inside the following words, running across the gap

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, the a, and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A bombardier has been shot in the chest.
explanation.definitionFit: A stab is an attempt, as in 'have a shot' or 'have a stab' at something.

clue.text: A line that can't be bettered in entertainment's signature tune?

annotation.answer: THERE'S NO BUSINESS LIKE SHOW BUSINESS

definitions.text: A line that can't be bettered in entertainment's signature tune?

blocks.clueFragment: A line that can't be bettered
blocks.note: surface reading: an unbeatable remark or slogan
setter's reading: the song that is showbiz's anthem, whose title line claims no trade beats the stage

explanation.walkthrough: The Irving Berlin song from Annie Get Your Gun is the anthem of showbiz, and its title line literally says that no other business can better it.
explanation.definitionFit: The song is the theme of the entertainment world, and its title is a boast that nothing tops the stage.

clue.text: See 7
See 7
Hold and study article cast in metal

indicators.note: casting something in metal sets it inside, so the article goes within the metal

blocks.note: to con is an old word for to study or learn
a metallic element
the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A craftsman holds and examines an object set in metal.
explanation.walkthrough: To con, meaning to study or learn by heart, is an old usage that crosswords keep alive.
explanation.definitionFit: To contain something is to hold it within, as a jug holds water.

clue.text: Female having the potential to succeed

definitions.text: Female having the potential to succeed

blocks.clueFragment: Female having the potential to succeed
blocks.note: surface reading: a promising woman likely to do well in her career
setter's reading: succeed in the sense of take over from someone, inheriting their estate or title

explanation.walkthrough: 'Succeed' looks like 'achieve success', but here it means follow on as the inheritor.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman entitled to inherit is the one in line to follow the holder into the property or title.

clue.text: Attempt to get money out of don entertaining the crowd

definitions.text: Attempt to get money out of

indicators.note: a host entertaining guests has them inside the house, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: to don clothing is to put it on
taken as written
a squeeze is a crush of people, a crowded gathering

explanation.surface: A university don hosts a crowd in an attempt to extract cash from them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don' reads as an Oxbridge tutor, but it is the verb meaning to wear, and its phrasal form opens to admit the other words.
explanation.definitionFit: To put the squeeze on someone is to pressure them, typically for payment or a favour.

clue.text: Bloomer over getting child in free

indicators.note: getting something in means receiving it inside, so one piece holds the other

blocks.note: O is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for an over
to rid is to free of something
standard abbreviation for child

explanation.surface: A mistake is made over freeing a trapped child.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomer' reads as a blunder but means something that blooms. O comes first, then RID holds CH: O-R(CH)ID.
explanation.definitionFit: An orchid is a flowering plant, so in crossword terms it is a bloomer, something that blooms.

clue.text: Embarrassed, old woman producing drink containing meths

blocks.note: red-faced with embarrassment
biddy is informal, rather unkind slang for an old woman

explanation.surface: An embarrassed old lady is caught making moonshine laced with meths.
explanation.definitionFit: Red biddy is British slang for cheap red wine fortified with methylated spirits, drunk by down-and-outs.

clue.text: Jazz pianist making brilliant appearance, first to last

indicators.note: the opening letter is taken off the front and moved to the end of the word

blocks.note: a shine is a gleam or brilliant look

explanation.surface: A jazz pianist makes a dazzling appearance in the opening number.
explanation.definitionFit: Earl 'Fatha' Hines was a hugely influential American jazz pianist of the swing era.

clue.text: A pass splitting the French in game

indicators.note: to split something is to wedge into it, so one piece sits between the letters of the other

blocks.note: le is French for 'the'
taken as written
in football a cross is a pass across the field

explanation.surface: A pass splits the French defence during a match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In game' reads as describing where the pass happens, but 'game' alone is the definition; the article and the pass together sit inside the French word.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacrosse is a team sport played with netted sticks, so it is a game.

clue.text: Industrial region - seediest, possibly

indicators.note: possibly signals one possible arrangement of the word's letters among many

blocks.note: every letter is used

explanation.surface: A rather unkind remark that an industrial area might be the shabbiest.
explanation.definitionFit: Teesside, around Middlesbrough in north-east England, was a centre of steel and chemical industry.

clue.text: Winning a crown

blocks.note: taken as written
the crown is the top of the head

explanation.surface: A victorious monarch wins a crown.
explanation.definitionFit: A team that is ahead is leading the contest, currently winning.

clue.text: Motion initially to wife, inside playing music

indicators.note: initially means only the opening letter of the word is used
inside places the preceding pair of pieces within the following one

blocks.note: the first letter
a show that is on is being played
taken as written
standard abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: A meeting motion is put to the wife, while music plays indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inside' acts on both 'to' and 'wife' together, which go into the word for playing after the initial letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Motown is the Detroit record label whose soul-pop sound became a genre of music in its own right.

clue.text: Astute running secures bronze

indicators.note: running suggests letters set in motion and scattered into a different order

blocks.note: every letter is used

explanation.surface: A shrewd runner wins third place in the race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bronze' reads as the third-place medal, but it is a cast sculpture.
explanation.definitionFit: A bronze is a sculpture cast in that metal, so a statue.

clue.text: Holiday in a secluded spot

blocks.note: first meaning: a break from work, as when Parliament or school stops sitting
second meaning: an alcove or hidden nook

explanation.surface: Someone spends their holiday tucked away somewhere quiet.
explanation.definitionFit: A recess is both a period when a body such as Parliament adjourns and a hollow set back in a wall.

clue.text: You'll need to get a round in before playing this dangerous game

definitions.text: You'll need to get a round in before playing this dangerous game

blocks.clueFragment: You'll need to get a round in before playing
blocks.note: surface reading: buying drinks for everyone at the pub before a game
setter's reading: load a single bullet into the revolver's chamber

explanation.walkthrough: 'Get a round in' is pub talk for buying drinks, but the round here is a cartridge loaded into a gun.
explanation.definitionFit: The deadly game involves a revolver loaded with one cartridge, spun and fired at one's own head.

clue.text: Revolutionary line number brought over

indicators.note: brought over means turned over, so the number is read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for line
a number

explanation.surface: A revolutionary leader's line and number are brought over.
explanation.definitionFit: Vladimir Lenin led the Bolshevik Revolution in Russia in 1917.

clue.text: Saying about young goat on deserted mountain

indicators.note: about means going around, so the first word encloses the others

blocks.note: a saw is an old proverb or saying
a kid is a young goat
D is an abbreviation for deserted

explanation.surface: A proverb about a young goat stranded on a lonely peak.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'on' simply means followed by. Skiddaw is a mountain in the Lake District of north-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Skiddaw is one of the highest fells in England's Lake District, overlooking Keswick.

clue.text: In which one may eat meals daughter and I take home close to nine

definitions.text: In which one may eat meals

indicators.note: close to means the closing letter of the word is the one used

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for daughter
taken as written
nett pay is what one takes home after deductions
the last letter

explanation.surface: A daughter and I get home shortly before nine for dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take home' looks like a verb but is the noun phrase take-home pay, NETT in British spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: A dinette is a small dining area or alcove, a place in which meals are eaten.

clue.text: Competition's not finished yet

indicators.note: not finished means the word stops short, missing its final letter

blocks.note: an event is a competition, as in a sports meeting

explanation.surface: A competition hasn't ended yet.
explanation.definitionFit: Even and yet both act as intensifiers before comparatives, as in 'even better' or 'yet better'.

clue.text: Plants in garden Shay cultivated

blocks.note: every letter is used

explanation.surface: Shay has grown some plants in his garden.
explanation.definitionFit: Hydrangeas are flowering shrubs with large rounded flower heads, common garden plants.
